title: The faces in the clouds
text: Humans see faces everywhere: in electrical sockets, cliff faces, the moon, the front of a car. The habit appears to be {{1}} (BIOLOGY) hard-wired, since no culture is exempt and even babies preferentially track face-like patterns. Psychologists call the illusion pareidolia, and it is less a glitch than an {{2}} (EXCEED) useful shortcut. Our ancestors survived by noticing predators and rivals instantly, so a detection system that is quick to {{3}} (FALSE) accuse a rock of being a face beats a cautious one that misses an enemy. The brain even devotes a special region to the job, one that responds to faces with astonishing {{4}} (SENSITIVE): starve it of real faces, experiments suggest, and it grows {{5}} (INCREASE) eager, finding them in static, clouds and toast. Manufacturers understand the instinct perfectly — car grilles are sculpted into smiles and scowls, giving machines an oddly {{6}} (LIFE) countenance — and ghost-hunters' audio recordings are largely the {{7}} (HEAR) version of the same illusion, finding whispers in hiss. Far from being a malfunction, all of this is the running cost of a social species: a brain so eager for faces will occasionally {{8}} (APPOINT) us, but it is also the reason we recognise our friends instantly, in poor light, at fifty paces.

gaps.explanation: 'appears to be biologically hard-wired' — adverb from biology.
'an exceedingly useful shortcut' — adverb from exceed.
'quick to falsely accuse a rock' — adverb from false.
'the hearing version of the illusion' — noun from hear.
'will occasionally disappoint us' — negative prefix dis-.
